mcqs.question: Why does backpropagation start at the output layer and work backward, rather than starting at the input layer?
options: Because forward-direction gradient computation is mathematically impossible
Because it is computationally identical to working forward, just implemented in reverse for convenience
Because input-layer weights don't need gradients
Because the loss is only defined at the output, so gradients must originate there and propagate back via the chain rule
mcqs.explanation: The loss is computed at the output, so the chain rule naturally starts there and propagates the gradient backward layer by layer to every weight, including the earliest ones, which very much do need gradients. It's not just a stylistic reversal — it directly follows from where the loss is defined.

mcqs.question: What makes backpropagation efficient compared to computing each weight's gradient independently from scratch?
options: It reuses each layer's already-computed gradient as a shared factor for every weight feeding into that layer
It skips computing gradients for most layers
It approximates gradients instead of computing them exactly
It only works when the network has a single hidden layer
mcqs.explanation: The chain rule lets a layer's gradient, computed once, be reused across all the weights feeding into it, bringing total cost down to roughly one forward-pass equivalent instead of one computation per weight. Backprop computes exact gradients (given the graph) and works for networks of any depth.

mcqs.question: Training loss on a 50-layer network has been completely flat for many epochs despite lowering the learning rate. What should you check first?
options: Increase the number of epochs further, since deep networks just need more time
Inspect per-layer gradient magnitudes for vanishing or exploding gradients
Switch to a smaller batch size, since that always fixes flat loss
Add more training data, since flat loss always means insufficient data
mcqs.explanation: A flat loss on a very deep network is a classic vanishing-or-exploding-gradient symptom, which a smaller learning rate does not fix — the actual gradient magnitude reaching early layers needs to be inspected directly. More epochs, a different batch size, or more data address different problems and won't resolve a genuinely vanished gradient.
